Americans who lose their jobs these days are facing a harsh new problem: It's getting harder to find another one quickly.
The average jobless worker's bout of unemployment surpassed 27 weeks in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, according to Friday's jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That amounts to a job search of nearly seven months, the longest outside of the pandemic period since 2016, when the U.S. labor market was finally getting back on track after the 2008 financial crisis.
About 2 million Americans have been without work for at least 27 weeks, the BLS reported. People in this category are referred to as the "long-term unemployed" and accounted for 27.6% of all jobless workers in October, the highest share since late 2021.
"This is a series that can be noisy from month to month," said Cory Stahle, senior economist at Indeed, a hiring platform. "But if you look over a longer time horizon, there is no mistake in the trend."
It's a troubling sign in an otherwise steady labor market. Workers stuck on the sidelines are a casualty of what's become a "low-hire, low-fire" job market, in which companies are hesitant to lay workers off, but aren't adding them either.
Research shows that Americans who experience long-term unemployment face depleted savings, lower earnings potential over time and declining mental health.
What's more, workers who are unemployed for extended periods risk falling into a self-perpetuating cycle, researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond wrote earlier this year.
"Time spent unemployed may itself reduce the probability of finding a job, perhaps because skills depreciate, networks thin or employers interpret long unemployment durations as a negative signal," the researchers warned.
Workers stop being able to claim most, if not all, government unemployment benefits after 26 weeks in a year. Given that, a rising share of long-term unemployed people can explain in part why initial and continuing jobless claims have remained low.
"Now, the average unemployed person takes longer to find a job than their benefits would last," Stahle said. "That is a really key point of this."
A 'jarring' narrative
While jobless workers appear to be having a tough time, this week's employment data shows strength in other areas of the labor market.
Nonfarm payrolls blew past economists' forecasts for October and added 165,000 jobs, according to Friday's release. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%, slightly lower than economists predicted.
Job openings came in much higher than economists expected in September, according to a separate report from the BLS released on Tuesday. The number of workers quitting jobs — a barometer of their confidence to obtain new employment — spiked to levels not seen since March 2025.
The BLS also said layoffs and discharges dropped to their lowest volume in more than a year. However, a recent string of high-profile workforce cuts could throw cold water on views among workers that the market is heating up.

Kim was up by more than 400,000 votes as of Friday afternoon.

Shortly after the New York City Marathon, tragic news broke: A 24-year-old runner, Rachel Apa, collapsed on the course and died in the hospital after doctors worked for six hours to save her life, according to the New York Times. Apa’s father told NYT the cause of death was rhabdomyolysis (a.k.a. rhabdo).
The news is shocking and saddening—as well as unsettling. Questions are popping up from runners on social media as to how something like this could happen to a young woman who was reportedly a former Division I field hockey player at Bucknell University and had spent months training for the marathon.
To help answer some of those questions, we talked to doctors to explain what runners need to know about rhabdo, and how to stay safe.
What Is Rhabdo?
First, know that rhabdo is relatively rare and dying from it is even rarer. Approximately 26,000 cases of rhabdomyolysis are reported annually in the United States, and the mortality rate starts at 10 percent but may go up to 50 percent in severe cases.
In short, rhabdo is a breakdown of muscle that in and of itself is not life-threatening. In fact, Derek M. Fine, MD, a nephrologist at Johns Hopkins Medicine, says that if you were to test creatine kinase (a.k.a. CK, a blood marker of muscle breakdown) in marathon runners after the race, “most” of them would show elevated levels of the enzyme.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says that multiple CK tests are the only way to accurately identify rhabdo, though. Normal CK is between 20 and 200 U/L, but rhabdo is diagnosed when it reaches five times the upper limit.
“There’s always a little bit of muscle breakdown and the reason is because, at least in [a] marathon, you’re using the muscles so much that at some point they can run out of an energy supply,” Fine says, adding that the mitochondria can't keep up and make enough of what’s called ATP (adenosine triphosphate), which is your primary source of energy.
Why Is It So Dangerous?
Rhabdo becomes dangerous when it becomes more severe. As muscle tissue breaks down, the body can release harmful substances into the bloodstream, including myoglobin, a protein that can damage the kidneys, and excessive amounts of potassium.
As for myoglobin, the protein can get “stuck” in the kidney and cause kidney failure or injury at various levels, Fine says. “It can be quite severe, but that usually takes a little bit of time to manifest,” he explains.
Fine says that high levels of potassium are probably a bigger risk than myoglobin. “When the muscle cells break up, you get a very large release of potassium into the bloodstream and that potassium then can cause cardiac arrhythmias,” he says. This can cause kidney failure (your kidneys are the organ tasked with getting rid of extra potassium) or potentially sudden cardiac arrest.
“Under normal circumstances, if it’s happening slowly and you’ve got decent kidneys, you pee the potassium out and it never gets that high in the blood,” he says. “If there's severe rhabdo and you have a huge amount of muscles breaking down, you can release a ton of potassium and your body can't get rid of it fast enough.”
In addition to the rapid release of these substances, rhabdo can sometimes lead to other issues that resemble sepsis or even multisystem organ failure, Fine says.

Data centers are unpopular — and a powerful motor of economic growth, experts say
The shifting political winds surrounding data centers could buffet the entire U.S. economy, reducing investment in artificial intelligence and slowing growth, according to Wall Street analysts.
The historic tide of money pouring into AI, from data centers and frontier models to state-of-the-art chips and networking gear, has boosted business investment and financial markets in recent years. Federal Reserve researchers recently estimated that spending on data centers, power facilities and other AI-related tech equipment accounted for roughly 20% of U.S. gross domestic product over the preceding year.
In 2026, spending by "hyperscalers" such as Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft — the companies racing to build data centers — is set to double to around $800 billion and is expected to reach $1 trillion in 2027, according to Capital Economics. Although slowing that buildout might well serve the public interest, given the widespread opposition to data centers, crimping that flow of dollars will have knock-on economic effects.
"Our economy is leveraged on this idea that AI will make us rich," economist Allison Schrager with the Manhattan Institute, a nonpartisan think tank, told CBS News. "There are risks to making it slower — it will mean slower growth."
"Detrimental effects"
Economists and investors now expect the Democrats' sweeping midterm election wins to both slow and increase the cost of data center development across the U.S. By contrast, those victories are unlikely to completely turn off the spigot, experts said, noting that political opposition to data centers isn't uniform, ranging from support for moratoriums on construction to more moderate proposals.
As a result, investment in data centers is likely to continue in the near term, both for projects currently underway and for facilities that have received permits.
For companies investing in AI, the bigger issue will be continuing such capital expenditures at the same pace even as the productivity gains and profits AI is expected to deliver remain largely unrealized for now.
"The high-level calculations essential to justify that level of CapEx, if sustained, we are talking $2 trillion in revenue for major AI companies by the early 2030s, which seems very unlikely," Capital Economics chief North America economist Stephen Brown told CBS News. "Our view is that because of that, there is likely to be some slowdown in data center construction. We are not saying it will stop altogether, but the level of investment is likely to ease. And that would have some detrimental effects on the U.S. economy."
Impact on stocks and consumer spending
Moody's Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi thinks investors are willing to continue pouring money into AI for the next couple of years, but said the long-term prospects are less clear.
"There are a lot of questions about whether that capital will continue to be there to fill that hole and, if not, AI companies will have to raise prices to cover costs. Then you won't see the same kind of investment," he said.
In 2025, investment in AI added roughly 0.3 percentage points to real GDP growth, according to Capital Economics, which expects investment in the sector to boost growth by roughly the same amount this year.

Bank of America earlier saw the limit would be reached around May.
The US government is less than $800 billion shy of its $41.1 trillion borrowing cap. Treasury's estimates released last week call for roughly $800 billion of net borrowing in the January-to-March period. The department also projected an end-March cash balance of $1 trillion, a record quarter-end target.
The Treasury's increased cash balance likely reflects greater reliance on short-term bills to finance government spending and deficits. Because bill issuance results in larger and more frequent cash outflows during the month, officials generally seek to maintain a larger buffer. That, in turn, uses up the remaining borrowing capacity at a faster rate.
Unless there is an agreement by Congress to raise or suspend the debt limit, the Treasury can avoid breaching it by deploying extraordinary accounting measures that could add an estimated $300 billion to $350 billion before it runs the risk of default.
Strategists, including SMBC Nikko Securities America, expect that the so-called X date — the point at which the Treasury exhausts funds from its cash balance and extraordinary measures and is no longer able to meet all of its obligations — to be sometime between August and November.
The Democratic sweep of Congress raises the prospect of a prolonged confrontation with President Donald Trump over the government's borrowing.
Fitch Ratings warned last month that such an outcome would increase the likelihood of brinkmanship, unless the outgoing Republican-led Congress manages to raise or suspend the debt ceiling before its term expires at year's end.
Debt-limit constraints tend to ripple through funding markets as the Treasury begins drawing down its cash balance and reducing bill issuance. While that temporarily increases reserves in the banking system, putting downward pressure on overnight funding rates, those effects typically reverse once the debt ceiling is resolved. The Treasury will then ramp up bill issuance to replenish its coffers, draining reserves and driving funding costs

Component Prices and Demand Drive Growth

“If we had gotten our hands on more product, we would have sold more,” Agrawal said, describing demand as “extremely strong.”
Austen said Components book-to-bill ratios remained well above parity and backlog extended into mid-2027. Lead times continued to increase, though they remained below levels associated with a pervasive shortage.

Turns out, I peaked around 30 to 35 miles for all three of those marathons. It made me realize there was room for growth.
When I got the opportunity to run New York again this year, I figured out how high I could go mileage-wise without upping my risk for injury.
I started by talking to Andrew Kastor, head coach of the Asics Mammoth Track Club. Before our call, I sent him the training plan I planned to follow for this upcoming training cycle: the Runner’s World Break Four Hours plan. (I also intended to continue strength training twice a week.)

This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Before the open on November 6, 2026, AST SpaceMobile (NASDAQ:ASTS) said it will build its own rocket, Blacklift, to launch its BlueBird satellites starting in late 2028. Firefly Aerospace (NASDAQ:FLY | FLY Price Prediction) will supply the engines.

Launching its own rocket would let AST rely less on SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX). The cost is a capital-heavy rocket program at a company still working to get its satellites into orbit and earn revenue.
What AST Actually Committed To
AST says Blacklift is designed to be reused and to carry up to five BlueBirds per launch. The company’s headline calls it a 20-ton rocket but does not say whether that number refers to payload.
The rocket does not exist yet, and the late-2028 target is ambitious. AST plans to unveil it in New York on November 12.
AST gets a permanent license to build Firefly’s Miranda engine and Vira, its vacuum version, at a new U.S. engine plant. President Scott Wisniewski said Miranda lets AST “leapfrog the traditional five-to-ten-year development cycle.”
How AST Pays for Its Engines
Firefly Aerospace values the deal at more than $1.3 billion over three years. That covers 27 Miranda and nine Vira engines for AST’s first three rockets, plus the license and engineering support. Firefly keeps engine intellectual property.
The license costs about $800 million upfront: $400 million in cash plus 10 million to 14 million AST Class A shares. The share count depends on a forward volume-weighted average price, the stock’s average trading price over a future period weighted by volume. If AST’s stock is weaker during that period, Firefly gets more shares.
AST then pays $250 million for engines and $250 million for three years of engineering support. The shares come with lock-ups, but they still dilute current holders.
Why Firefly Posted Its Biggest Gain Since Its Debut
By daily closes, this was Firefly’s biggest gain since it began trading on August 7, 2025. It beat the 22.8% gain on December 19, 2025, and the 34.1% first-day rise above its IPO price.
The jump shows the deal’s size, which is worth about 37% of Firefly’s $3.48 billion market value and about 4.5 times its trailing revenue of $287.01 million.
Even after the jump, the stock sits about 54% below its $45 IPO price. Firefly reports on November 10 and will discuss the deal on a 5 p.m. ET call.
Where AST’s Rocket Plan Could Stall
AST has bought launches from SpaceX, India’s space agency, and Blue Origin. It still holds launch agreements covering more than 100 BlueBirds through 2027 and 2028. Blacklift would help AST rely less on those providers, and the release names no provider it plans to drop.
Rocket programs often slip. This one adds cash burn and dilution at a company that lost $230.91 million in the second quarter, and it could take attention away from putting satellites in orbit, which is the business that has to produce revenue.

Inheriting a 401(k) stuffed with company stock sounds like a windfall until the standard rollover form arrives. One signature can decide whether nearly $2 million gets taxed at the highest rates, and most heirs only learn the alternative after it's…
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
If your parent left you a 401(k) full of company stock, the default paperwork could cost you a fortune. A little-known IRS rule called net unrealized appreciation (NUA) lets an heir take employer stock out of an inherited 401(k) and pay capital gains tax on most of it instead of ordinary income tax. Most heirs never hear about it until the money has already moved.
A Hypothetical $2 Million Inheritance Inside a 401(k)
This example is hypothetical. It exists to show how the rule works. A son, 52, is the named beneficiary of his late father’s 401(k). The father spent 33 years as a systems engineer at IBM (NYSE:IBM | IBM Price Prediction) and bought IBM stock inside the plan throughout his career. Those purchases, plus IBM’s two-for-one stock splits declared in January 1997 and January 1999 (per IBM’s filings), left the plan holding 8,000 shares with a cost basis of $231,000.
At IBM’s price of $244.89 as of 2:37 PM ET on Nov. 6, 2026, the shares are worth $1,959,120. That leaves $1,728,120 of net unrealized appreciation, or 88.2% of the position. The value moves with IBM’s stock price.
Two Paths, Two Very Different Tax Bills
The default: an inherited IRA. Most heirs roll the balance into an inherited IRA. The son is more than 10 years younger than his father, so he falls outside the eligible designated beneficiary category for someone “not more than 10 years younger” than the owner. That means he must empty the account by the end of the tenth year after the year his father died, per the IRS. Every dollar he withdraws, growth included, counts as ordinary income.
The overlooked option: a lump-sum distribution. The IRS treats a payout made “Because of the plan participant’s death” as a lump-sum distribution if the entire balance comes out within a single tax year. The son takes the IBM shares in kind, moving them as stock into a taxable brokerage account. IRS Publication 575 explains the result: “employer stock basis is taxed as ordinary income and appreciation is taxed later at capital gains rates.” The NUA “is generally tax free until you sell or exchange the securities.”
In this example, he reports $231,000 as ordinary income in the year of the distribution. The $1,728,120 of appreciation goes untaxed until he sells. At that point, The CPA Journal notes, it counts as a long-term capital gain.
Where the Rule Lives in the Tax Code
NUA treatment comes from 26 U.S.C. § 402(e)(4), which covers employer securities paid out of qualified plans. IRS Publication 575 lays out how it works. The CPA Journal points out how easy it is to miss: “NUA can frequently be overlooked when taxpayers look to consolidate older plans into one IRA or even at death when an heir is named the designated beneficiary of the plan.”

Starwood Property Trust NYSE: STWD will review its dividend with its board after higher interest rates increased pressure on some borrowers and contributed to a sharp rise in loan-loss reserves, Chairman and CEO Barry Sternlicht said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call.
The real estate investment trust reported distributable earnings of $0.31 per share for the quarter, or $0.41 per share excluding realized gains and losses from commercial lending resolutions. Sternlicht said the dividend had been paid above the earnings rates the company produced in recent quarters and that management would consider whether to reduce it and increase it later as earnings recover.
“I think there is a question of prudency,” Sternlicht said. No dividend decision was announced on the call.
President Jeff DiModica said the company had previously seen a path to earning the $0.48 per share it was paying out within a few quarters. He said current projections were at or slightly above the $0.41 adjusted distributable earnings figure, based on what the company knows today. Sternlicht called that figure a reasonable base earnings rate, while saying he hoped it would rise as capital is returned to productive investments.
Higher Rates Drive Reserve Increase
Chief Financial Officer Rina Paniry said reserves against commercial lending non-accrual loans and real estate owned increased by $369 million during the quarter. The total comprised $822 million in current expected credit loss, or CECL, reserves and $217 million in reserves on real estate owned. Those reserves were reflected in undepreciated book value of $17.22 per share.
DiModica said most of the increase was driven by higher interest rates incorporated into a third-party model. Higher projected rates can increase borrowers’ debt-service costs and reduce refinancing proceeds, even when property operations improve, he said. Substantially all of the increase was in the general reserve.
The balance of loans rated four increased by $290 million, while five-rated loans rose by $440 million. All downgrades during the quarter involved loans originated before 2023, and more than half involved multifamily properties, DiModica said.
Asked where reserves might go from here, DiModica said the company could not predict the outcome, noting that management had not expected the quarter’s reserve build before the rate move. Sternlicht said the CECL calculation was a mechanical exercise based on the model.
Legacy Asset Resolutions Continue
Starwood resolved $254 million of non-accrual loans and real estate owned during the quarter, Paniry said. That included the sale of two multifamily properties with an aggregate distributable earnings basis of $134 million for $97 million, as well as the sale of two units in a New York City residential project for $12 million. The sales were completed in cash without seller financing.
The company also returned the final $108 million portion of a Brooklyn office loan to accrual status after securing a lease that brought the property to full occupancy. DiModica said Starwood had restructured the loan to support leasing rather than pursue foreclosure.
There were no new non-accrual loans or foreclosures in the quarter, DiModica said. Management said it remained on track to exceed its previously stated $800 million resolution target for 2026, while Sternlicht cautioned that some assets could take longer to resolve than previously hoped.

President and CEO Eric Hambly said the company generated $515 million in operating cash flow during the quarter, with contributions from the Eagle Ford, Gulf of America and Tupper Montney assets. Bubale Appraisal Plans Take Shape
Murphy’s Bubale West-1X well confirmed oil in the Turonian reservoir down dip from the original discovery and encountered hydrocarbons in the deeper Albian reservoir, Hambly said. Pressure data suggest the Turonian reservoir is likely continuous between the two wells, which are about eight miles apart, although further work is needed to establish the extent and quality of the field.
Hambly said the West-1X well encountered both oil- and water-bearing Turonian sands. The water could represent an oil-water contact across the reservoir, but that remains unconfirmed. Murphy also found oil in the deeper Cenomanian and Albian reservoirs, which require further appraisal.
The CEO said preliminary screening suggests a standalone deepwater development using a floating production, storage and offloading vessel would require roughly more than 150 million barrels. He cautioned that the commercial threshold could change as Murphy learns more about reservoir quality and the number of wells needed.
Murphy expects to be better positioned to provide an updated resource range as it progresses appraisal over the next 18 to 24 months. Hambly said the company is seeking a rig and currently expects to start the next appraisal program in the second quarter of 2027, although the timing is not final.
